title: Pharmacokinetics: ADME
summary: How the body absorbs, distributes, metabolizes and eliminates drugs, and the numbers that describe it.

lessons.title: Absorption and Bioavailability

levels.kid:
Before a medicine can help you, it has to get into your blood. That trip is called **absorption**.

If you swallow a pill, it goes to your tummy and then your gut, where it soaks into the blood. But first the blood from the gut goes to the liver, and the liver is like a guard at a gate. It breaks some of the medicine down before it can travel around your body.

A shot straight into a vein skips the gate, so all of it gets in right away. That's why doctors sometimes use a shot when they need a medicine to work fast.
levels.hs:
**Absorption** is how a drug moves from where it's given into the bloodstream. The **route** matters:
- **Intravenous (IV)**: straight into the blood, so 100% gets in, instantly.
- **Oral**: swallowed, absorbed mostly in the small intestine, which has a huge surface area.
- **Intramuscular, subcutaneous, inhaled, transdermal (patch), sublingual (under the tongue)**: each has its own speed.

To be absorbed, most drugs must cross cell membranes, which are made of fat. Small, **fat-soluble** (lipophilic), **uncharged** molecules cross best. Many drugs are weak acids or weak bases, and whether they carry a charge depends on the pH around them.

**First-pass metabolism.** Blood from the gut travels through the **portal vein** to the liver before reaching the rest of the body. Enzymes in the gut wall and liver can destroy much of a swallowed drug before it ever circulates. Nitroglycerin is mostly destroyed this way, so it's given **under the tongue**, where it absorbs straight into veins that skip the liver.

**Bioavailability (F)** is the fraction of a dose that reaches the circulation unchanged. IV bioavailability is 100% by definition. Oral bioavailability can be anywhere from almost zero to nearly 100%. Food, other drugs and stomach acid can all change it; for example, calcium and iron bind certain antibiotics in the gut and block their absorption.
levels.college:
**Mechanisms of membrane passage.** Most drugs cross by **passive diffusion** down a concentration gradient (Fick's law: rate rises with surface area, gradient and lipid solubility, and falls with membrane thickness). Others use **carrier-mediated transport** (uptake by SLC transporters such as PEPT1 for some β-lactams and ACE inhibitors) or are pumped back out by **efflux transporters** such as P-glycoprotein. Large molecules may enter by endocytosis or paracellular routes.

**Ionization.** Only the un-ionized form diffuses readily. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation predicts the ratio:
- Weak acid: pH − pKa = log([A−]/[HA])
- Weak base: pKa − pH = log([BH+]/[B])
When pH equals pKa, the drug is 50% ionized. Weak acids are more un-ionized in acidic fluids and weak bases in alkaline ones. In practice most absorption of both happens in the small intestine, because its surface area and blood flow overwhelm the pH effect.

**Bioavailability.** F = AUC(oral) / AUC(IV), with equal doses (or dose-normalized). Oral F is reduced by incomplete dissolution, poor permeability, efflux, degradation, and **first-pass** extraction in the gut wall (CYP3A4 with P-gp) and liver. F(oral) ≈ fa × fg × fh, the fractions absorbed, surviving the gut wall, and surviving the liver.

**Key parameters.** Cmax (peak concentration), Tmax (time to peak) and AUC (total exposure). Two formulations are **bioequivalent** when the 90% confidence intervals for the ratios of their AUC and Cmax fall within 80–125%.

**Routes that avoid first pass**: IV, sublingual, buccal, transdermal, inhaled and (partly) rectal. Modified-release formulations slow absorption to smooth the curve.

**Interactions.** Polyvalent cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, Al3+, Fe2+) chelate tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones. Raising gastric pH reduces the absorption of drugs that need acid to dissolve, such as ketoconazole and some kinase inhibitors.
levels.phd:
Oral absorption is a multi-step process, and the **Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)** organizes it by two rate-limiting properties: solubility and intestinal permeability. Class I drugs (high solubility, high permeability) absorb well regardless of formulation. Class II drugs (low solubility, high permeability) are dissolution-limited, so particle size, salt form, amorphous dispersions and food (bile micelles) change exposure. Class III drugs (high solubility, low permeability) are permeability-limited, and class IV drugs are poor on both counts. The related BDDCS adds that highly permeable drugs tend to be cleared by metabolism and poorly permeable drugs by renal or biliary excretion, which helps predict transporter effects.

**The gut wall is an organ of elimination.** Enterocyte CYP3A4 and apical P-gp act together: P-gp effluxes drug back into the lumen, repeatedly exposing it to enterocyte metabolism. Grapefruit furanocoumarins irreversibly inactivate intestinal (not hepatic) CYP3A4. This explains why grapefruit greatly increases oral exposure of high-first-pass CYP3A4 substrates (such as felodipine and simvastatin) while barely affecting their IV kinetics.

**pH-partition theory** predicts **ion trapping**: at equilibrium, a weak base concentrates in the more acidic compartment, because the ionized form cannot diffuse back. The same principle explains weak base accumulation in acidic organelles (lysosomotropism, part of the high Vd of amines) and in breast milk, and the renal effect of urinary pH on reabsorption.

**Absorption kinetics** are often first-order with rate constant ka, but they can be zero-order (controlled-release systems) or saturable (carrier-mediated). When ka is slower than the elimination rate constant, **flip-flop kinetics** occur: the terminal slope reflects absorption rather than elimination. This is common with depot injections and some extended-release products, and it is easy to misread as a long elimination half-life.

**Regional differences.** Absorption windows in the proximal small intestine (for some drugs relying on uptake transporters) limit the benefit of extended-release formulations that move past that region before releasing drug.
levels.expert:
**Route selection is clinical reasoning.** In a vomiting, seizing or intubated patient, oral absorption is unreliable, so IV, intramuscular, intranasal or rectal routes are chosen. In status epilepticus, intramuscular midazolam performed as well as IV lorazepam in the RAMPART trial for prehospital use, because no IV access was needed. When converting between routes, bioavailability matters: oral levetiracetam is nearly completely absorbed, so oral and IV doses are interchangeable. Drugs with low oral F need very different oral and IV doses, and conversions should be checked rather than assumed.

**Gut function changes absorption.** Ileus, short bowel, gastric bypass surgery, enteral feeding tubes and critical illness all reduce or delay absorption. Continuous tube feeds bind some drugs: phenytoin levels classically fall when given with enteral nutrition, so feeds are often held around doses and levels monitored. Crushing extended-release tablets for a feeding tube can deliver the whole dose at once and cause toxicity; enteric-coated and extended-release formulations should not be crushed.

**Interaction pitfalls**
- Separate fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, levothyroxine and bisphosphonates from calcium, iron, magnesium and antacids.
- Proton pump inhibitors reduce absorption of drugs needing acid, including some tyrosine kinase inhibitors and ketoconazole.
- Grapefruit raises exposure of oral CYP3A4 substrates with high first pass.

**Formulation is pharmacology.** Swapping between extended-release brands or generics of narrow-therapeutic-index drugs (antiepileptics, tacrolimus, levothyroxine) can shift levels slightly, so consistency and monitoring are prudent when switching. Transdermal absorption rises with heat and fever, so a warmed patch, such as from a heating blanket, can deliver more drug than intended; fentanyl patches are the classic warning.

**First-pass loss can be clinically useful.** Drugs given rectally partly bypass the liver; sublingual and buccal routes bypass it completely. Knowing which route skips which barrier lets you predict onset and exposure.

keyPoints: Bioavailability (F) is the fraction of a dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged; IV F = 100%
F = AUC oral / AUC IV (dose-normalized)
First-pass metabolism in gut wall (CYP3A4, P-gp) and liver lowers oral F
Un-ionized, lipophilic drugs diffuse best; Henderson–Hasselbalch predicts ionization
Sublingual, transdermal, inhaled and IV routes avoid first pass
Polyvalent cations chelate tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones

test.q: Bioavailability is best defined as:
choices: The apparent volume of fluid the drug distributes into
The fraction of a dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged
The time it takes to reach peak plasma concentration
The rate at which the drug is eliminated from the body
test.explain: F is the fraction of administered drug that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.

test.q: By definition, the bioavailability of an IV dose is:
test.explain: IV drugs enter circulation directly, so F = 100% (1.0).

test.q: Why is nitroglycerin given sublingually for angina?
choices: It dissolves in saliva and is swallowed, which is faster than a tablet
Sublingual veins drain to the systemic circulation, bypassing first-pass liver metabolism
It needs to reach the lungs first, and sublingual veins drain to the airway
Stomach acid destroys nitrates, but salivary enzymes activate them
test.explain: Oral nitroglycerin undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism; sublingual absorption skips the portal circulation.

test.q: Which molecules cross cell membranes most easily by passive diffusion?
test.explain: Lipophilic, small, un-ionized molecules diffuse through the lipid bilayer best.

test.q: A weak acid with a pKa of 4 is placed in a fluid at pH 4. What fraction is ionized?
test.explain: When pH = pKa, ionized and un-ionized forms are equal (50% each).

test.q: Where does most oral drug absorption occur?
test.explain: The small intestine's enormous surface area and blood flow make it the main absorption site for weak acids and bases alike.

test.q: Blood from the gut reaches the liver first through the hepatic ___ vein.
test.explain: The portal vein carries absorbed drug to the liver, enabling first-pass metabolism.

test.q: Bioavailability is calculated as AUC(oral) divided by AUC(___), at equal doses.
test.explain: Comparing oral with IV exposure gives the fraction absorbed and surviving first pass.

test.q: Taking ciprofloxacin with a calcium supplement will most likely:
choices: Speed its excretion through the kidneys
Have no meaningful effect on its levels
Increase its absorption by raising gut pH
test.explain: Polyvalent cations chelate fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines in the gut.

test.q: Which route does NOT avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism?
test.explain: Oral drugs pass through the gut wall and liver before reaching the systemic circulation.

test.q: Name the efflux transporter in the gut wall that pumps many drugs back into the intestinal lumen. (abbreviation)
test.explain: P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) works with enterocyte CYP3A4 to limit oral absorption.

test.q: What abbreviation describes the time at which the peak plasma concentration occurs?
test.explain: Tmax is the time to reach Cmax, the peak concentration.

kidTest.q: Absorption means a medicine is getting into your:
kidTest.explain: Absorption is the trip into the bloodstream.

kidTest.q: Which body part acts like a guard at a gate for swallowed medicine?
kidTest.explain: The liver breaks down some medicine before it goes around the body.

kidTest.q: Which way gets ALL the medicine in right away?
kidTest.explain: IV medicine goes straight into the blood.

kidTest.q: A pill soaks into the blood mostly in your:
kidTest.explain: Most absorption happens in the small intestine.

kidTest.q: A shot into a vein skips the ___ gate. (one word)
kidTest.explain: IV drugs avoid first-pass metabolism in the liver.

advancedTest.q: Grapefruit juice markedly increases oral exposure to felodipine but barely changes IV kinetics. Why?
choices: It speeds gastric emptying so more drug reaches the small intestine
It inhibits hepatic CYP2D6, slowing felodipine's systemic clearance
It irreversibly inactivates intestinal CYP3A4, reducing gut-wall first pass
It displaces felodipine from albumin, raising the free drug fraction
advancedTest.explain: Furanocoumarins destroy enterocyte CYP3A4; hepatic CYP3A4 is little affected, so IV clearance is unchanged.

advancedTest.q: A depot injection shows a much longer terminal half-life than the same drug given IV. The likeliest explanation is:
choices: Flip-flop kinetics: slow absorption (ka < ke) governs the terminal slope
Saturated hepatic metabolism that slows clearance at depot doses
Enterohepatic recycling of drug excreted into bile from the depot
Reduced renal clearance caused by the depot's vehicle or excipients
advancedTest.explain: When absorption is slower than elimination, the terminal phase reflects absorption.

advancedTest.q: A BCS class II drug's exposure is most likely increased by:
choices: Taking it with a high-fat meal or using a formulation that improves dissolution
Giving it rectally to bypass the gut's dissolution problems
Taking it with an antacid so the stomach pH rises and it dissolves
Crushing it into plain water and drinking it on an empty stomach
advancedTest.explain: Class II drugs are solubility/dissolution-limited; bile micelles from food and enabling formulations help.

advancedTest.q: Why can crushing an extended-release opioid tablet for a feeding tube be dangerous?
choices: It increases first-pass metabolism so the drug stops working
It blocks the feeding tube permanently with sticky polymer
It releases the full dose at once, producing a toxic peak
It inactivates the opioid by exposing it to stomach acid
advancedTest.explain: Destroying the release mechanism causes dose dumping.

lessons.title: Distribution and Volume of Distribution

levels.kid:
Once medicine is in the blood, the blood carries it all over your body, like a delivery truck. This is called **distribution**.

Some medicine stays mostly in the blood. Some medicine likes to leave the blood and hide in fat or muscle, like a kid hiding in a big house.

Some medicine also holds hands with special helpers in the blood. While it's holding hands, it can't do its job. Only the medicine that is free can work.

Your brain has an extra-strong fence around it, so only some medicines can get in.
levels.hs:
**Distribution** is how a drug moves from the blood into the tissues. Three things control it:
- **Blood flow**: organs with lots of blood flow (brain, heart, liver, kidneys) get the drug first. Fat and resting muscle get it later.
- **Ability to cross membranes**: fat-soluble drugs leave the blood easily. Large or charged drugs stay in the blood.
- **Binding**: many drugs stick to blood proteins, mainly **albumin**. Only the **free (unbound)** drug can leave the blood, reach the target, and be cleared.

**Volume of distribution (Vd)** is a calculated number that tells you how widely a drug spreads:

Vd = amount of drug in the body ÷ plasma concentration

If a drug stays in the blood, the plasma concentration is high and Vd is **small**. If a drug soaks into tissues, little is left in the plasma, so Vd is **large**. Vd can be far bigger than the whole body, which is why it's called an "apparent" volume. It is not a real space.

The **blood–brain barrier** is made of tightly sealed capillaries plus pumps that push drugs back out. Only small, fat-soluble drugs (or drugs with special carriers) get into the brain well. That matters a lot for brain infections, tumors and anesthesia.
levels.college:
**Determinants.** Distribution depends on organ perfusion, capillary permeability, lipophilicity, ionization, and binding to plasma proteins and tissues. At equilibrium, unbound concentrations are equal across membranes for passively diffusing drugs (unless pH differences or transporters intervene).

**Plasma protein binding.** **Albumin** binds mainly acidic and neutral drugs (warfarin, phenytoin, NSAIDs). **α1-acid glycoprotein**, an acute-phase protein, binds many basic drugs (lidocaine, propranolol). The **fraction unbound (fu)** determines what is pharmacologically active and what is available to filtration and metabolism.

**Apparent volume of distribution.** Vd = dose / C0 (the plasma concentration extrapolated to time zero after an IV bolus). Reference volumes for a 70 kg adult: plasma about 3 L, extracellular fluid about 14 L, total body water about 42 L.
- **Small Vd** (near plasma volume): heparin, large proteins and monoclonal antibodies, and highly albumin-bound drugs such as warfarin.
- **Intermediate Vd** (body water): small polar molecules such as lithium spread through total body water.
- **Large Vd** (far above body water): amiodarone, chloroquine, digoxin, tricyclic antidepressants. These bind extensively to tissue.

A useful relation: Vd = Vp + Vt × (fu / fu,t), where Vp is plasma volume, Vt tissue volume and fu,t the tissue unbound fraction. Vd rises when tissue binding exceeds plasma binding.

**Barriers.** The blood–brain barrier (endothelial tight junctions, P-gp and BCRP efflux, astrocytic support) excludes polar molecules. Inflammation (as in meningitis) loosens it, which is why penicillin reaches CSF better when the meninges are inflamed. The placenta lets most lipophilic small molecules through.

**Redistribution.** After a bolus of a lipophilic drug such as propofol or thiopental, the brain equilibrates rapidly, then drug moves out to muscle and fat. Awakening from a single bolus is due to **redistribution**, not elimination.
levels.phd:
**Vd is a proportionality constant, not an anatomical space.** It links an amount to a measured concentration, and its value depends on which concentration is measured (total vs unbound, plasma vs blood). Multi-compartment drugs have several volumes: the central volume (Vc), the volume at steady state (Vss), which reflects true equilibrium partitioning, and Vβ (or Vz), which depends on the terminal slope and therefore on clearance. Vss is the physiologically meaningful one. Vβ always exceeds Vss and can change with clearance even if tissue binding does not, a common source of confusion in reported parameters.

**Tissue partitioning mechanisms.** Lipophilic amines achieve huge Vd through phospholipid binding and lysosomal ion trapping (lysosomotropism): the un-ionized base diffuses into acidic lysosomes, becomes protonated and is trapped. This underlies drug-induced phospholipidosis (amiodarone) and very long terminal half-lives. Digoxin's large Vd reflects binding to Na+/K+-ATPase in skeletal muscle, which is why lean body mass (not total weight) predicts its loading requirement.

**Protein binding: what really matters.** Displacement interactions were long overemphasized. For a low-extraction, restrictively cleared drug given chronically, displacement raises fu, which increases clearance proportionally, so the unbound steady-state concentration (the active one) returns to its previous value. Total concentration falls. The clinically meaningful consequences are mostly **interpretive**: in hypoalbuminemia, uremia or pregnancy, a "low" total phenytoin level may hide a normal or high free level. Displacement matters more for drugs given IV with high extraction and narrow therapeutic index, and transiently during the change.

**Barrier transport.** CNS exposure is better described by Kp,uu (the unbound brain-to-unbound plasma concentration ratio) than by total brain-to-plasma ratios, which are inflated by nonspecific lipid binding. A Kp,uu near one implies passive equilibration; well below one implies active efflux; above one implies active uptake. Many CNS drug failures trace to efflux-limited Kp,uu despite favorable total brain levels.
levels.expert:
**Distribution explains several bedside phenomena.**

**Loading doses depend on Vd.** Drugs with large Vd (amiodarone, digoxin, phenytoin) need a loading dose to reach target concentrations quickly. Weight-based dosing must use the right weight: hydrophilic drugs (aminoglycosides, many neuromuscular blockers) distribute into lean tissue and ECF, so obesity calls for ideal or adjusted body weight. Lipophilic drugs may distribute into fat, prolonging their effect after infusions stop.

**Fluid shifts change concentrations.** Critically ill patients with capillary leak, large-volume resuscitation or burns have an expanded ECF. Hydrophilic antibiotics such as β-lactams and aminoglycosides then reach lower concentrations, risking underdosing in sepsis. Edema and ascites increase Vd for these drugs.

**Free levels in neurocritical care.** Phenytoin is highly albumin-bound. In a hypoalbuminemic ICU or neurosurgical patient, or with kidney failure, the total level underestimates the active free fraction. Free phenytoin levels are preferred when available; correction formulas are imperfect. Valproate also displaces phenytoin and inhibits its metabolism, so combined use needs free levels.

**The blood–brain barrier sets drug choice.** For meningitis or ventriculitis, choose agents with good CSF penetration (third-generation cephalosporins, high-dose regimens, meropenem). Vancomycin penetrates modestly; aminoglycosides and some others penetrate poorly, which is one reason intraventricular administration exists for certain device-associated infections. Penetration falls as inflammation resolves, so early responses can be misleading. Corticosteroids, by restoring barrier integrity, can also reduce antibiotic entry into the CSF.

**Redistribution and context.** A single propofol bolus wears off quickly by redistribution. After a long infusion, peripheral tissues are saturated and recovery depends more on elimination. This is the concept of context-sensitive half-time, and it matters when planning a neurologic exam after sedation.

keyPoints: Distribution depends on blood flow, membrane permeability and binding
Only unbound (free) drug is active and available for elimination
Albumin binds acidic drugs; α1-acid glycoprotein binds many basic drugs
Vd = amount in body / plasma concentration; it is an apparent volume
Large Vd = extensive tissue binding (amiodarone, digoxin, TCAs); small Vd = stays in plasma (heparin, antibodies)
The blood–brain barrier uses tight junctions and efflux pumps (P-gp)

test.q: Which form of a drug can leave the blood and act on its target?
test.explain: Only free drug crosses membranes, binds targets and is filtered or metabolized.

test.q: The main plasma protein binding acidic drugs such as warfarin is:
test.explain: Albumin binds acidic and neutral drugs; α1-acid glycoprotein binds many basic drugs.

test.q: A drug has a very large Vd (far larger than total body water). This most likely means:
choices: It is highly bound to plasma albumin
It stays mostly in the plasma water
It is rapidly excreted by the kidney
It is extensively bound to tissues
test.explain: High tissue binding lowers plasma concentration and inflates the apparent Vd.

test.q: Which drug is classically confined largely to the plasma (small Vd)?
test.explain: Heparin is large and charged and stays mostly in the vascular space.

test.q: Vd is calculated as:
choices: Plasma concentration ÷ the dose that was given
Amount of drug in the body ÷ plasma concentration
Dose × bioavailability for an oral formulation
Clearance × half-life measured after an IV dose
test.explain: Vd = amount / concentration (for an IV bolus, dose / C0).

test.q: Why do patients wake quickly after a single bolus of propofol?
choices: Rapid renal excretion of unchanged drug
Redistribution from brain to muscle and fat
Most of the drug is exhaled through the lungs
Liver metabolism that finishes within seconds
test.explain: Brain concentrations fall as the drug redistributes to less-perfused tissues.

test.q: Volume of distribution is called an '___' volume because it does not correspond to a real body space.
test.explain: Vd is a proportionality constant and can exceed total body volume.

test.q: Tight junctions plus efflux pumps form the blood–___ barrier.
test.explain: The BBB restricts entry of polar drugs into the CNS.

test.q: Which organs receive a distributed drug first?
choices: The skin and subcutaneous tissue before the internal organs
Fat and bone, because they hold the most lipophilic drug
Well-perfused organs such as brain, heart, liver and kidney
Each tissue at a similar rate, regardless of blood flow
test.explain: Initial distribution follows blood flow.

test.q: In a patient with low albumin, a total phenytoin level reported as 'normal' may:
choices: Mean the drug is not absorbed
test.explain: With less albumin, a larger fraction is free; total levels underestimate active drug.

test.q: Name the acute-phase plasma protein that binds many basic drugs such as lidocaine. (three words, Greek letter can be written 'alpha')
test.explain: α1-acid glycoprotein rises in inflammation and binds basic drugs.

test.q: Do drugs with a large Vd usually need a loading dose to reach target levels quickly: yes or no?
test.explain: Loading dose = target concentration × Vd / F, so a larger Vd means a larger initial amount is needed.

kidTest.q: After medicine gets in the blood, the blood carries it like a:
kidTest.explain: Blood delivers medicine around the body.

kidTest.q: Which medicine can do its job?
kidTest.explain: Only free (unbound) drug works.

kidTest.q: Some medicine likes to hide in:
kidTest.explain: Some drugs move into tissues like fat and muscle.

kidTest.q: Around your brain there is a:
kidTest.explain: The blood–brain barrier keeps many drugs out.

kidTest.q: The brain's strong fence is called the blood–brain ___.
kidTest.explain: It protects the brain from many chemicals.

advancedTest.q: A low-extraction, highly albumin-bound drug is displaced by a second drug during chronic therapy. What happens to its unbound steady-state concentration?
choices: It returns to about the same value because clearance rises with fu
It rises in proportion to the displacement and stays elevated
It falls well below baseline because free drug is cleared faster
It doubles at steady state, so the dosing rate should be halved
advancedTest.explain: For restrictively cleared drugs, CL ∝ fu, so Css,unbound = dosing rate / CLint,unbound is unchanged; total concentration falls.

advancedTest.q: Which parameter best indicates passive equilibration of unbound drug across the blood–brain barrier?
advancedTest.explain: Kp,uu compares unbound concentrations; values well below 1 suggest efflux.

advancedTest.q: Lipophilic amines such as amiodarone accumulate in tissues partly through:
choices: Lysosomal ion trapping and phospholipid binding
Tight albumin binding that holds the drug in tissue
Active renal reabsorption via organic cation carriers
advancedTest.explain: Weak bases are trapped in acidic lysosomes and bind phospholipids, producing large Vd and phospholipidosis.

advancedTest.q: Why do hydrophilic antibiotics often reach low concentrations early in septic shock?
choices: Increased plasma protein binding that leaves little free drug in tissue
Reduced renal blood flow that slows delivery of the drug to infected sites
Capillary leak and fluid resuscitation expand the ECF, increasing Vd
Increased hepatic first-pass metabolism driven by the inflammatory response
advancedTest.explain: An expanded extracellular volume dilutes hydrophilic drugs; augmented renal clearance can add to it.

lessons.title: Metabolism: Phase I and Phase II

levels.kid:
Your body has a clean-up crew, mostly in your liver. Its job is to change medicines so they can be washed out of your body in pee or poop.

The crew works in two steps. In step one, it snips or changes a little part of the medicine, like taking the wrapper off candy. In step two, it sticks on a big "handle" that makes the medicine easy to wash away, like putting a big tag on it.

Some medicines don't work until the crew changes them. They start out "asleep" and the liver wakes them up!
levels.hs:
**Metabolism** (biotransformation) chemically changes drugs, mostly in the **liver**. The goal is to turn fat-soluble drugs, which the kidneys would just reabsorb, into **water-soluble** products that can be excreted.

**Phase I reactions** add or expose a reactive group through **oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis**. Most oxidation is done by the **cytochrome P450 (CYP)** enzymes. A handful of them handle most drugs: CYP3A4 (the biggest share), CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP1A2.

**Phase II reactions** attach a large polar molecule (**conjugation**): glucuronic acid (glucuronidation, the most common), sulfate, an acetyl group, glutathione or a methyl group. Conjugates are usually inactive and easy to excrete.

Metabolism doesn't always inactivate a drug:
- **Prodrugs** are inactive until metabolized. Codeine becomes morphine through CYP2D6. Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 to become active.
- Some metabolites are **toxic**. In an acetaminophen overdose, the normal pathways are overwhelmed, more drug is turned into a toxic product called NAPQI, and it damages the liver once glutathione runs out. The antidote, N-acetylcysteine, restores glutathione.

Metabolism varies between people. Genes, age, liver disease and other drugs can speed it up or slow it down. Some drugs **induce** (increase) CYP enzymes, such as rifampin and carbamazepine. Others **inhibit** them, such as clarithromycin, azole antifungals and grapefruit juice.
levels.college:
**Phase I (functionalization).** Oxidations by CYP450 (hydroxylation, N- and O-dealkylation, S-oxidation, epoxidation), plus flavin-containing monooxygenases, monoamine oxidase, alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, and xanthine oxidase. Reductions (azo and nitro reduction) and hydrolysis by esterases and amidases. Esters such as succinylcholine, esmolol and remifentanil are hydrolyzed rapidly in plasma or tissues, giving very short actions.

**CYP isoforms**
- CYP3A4/5: the largest share of drugs; abundant in liver and enterocytes (macrolides, many statins, calcium channel blockers, benzodiazepines such as midazolam, calcineurin inhibitors).
- CYP2D6: many antidepressants, antipsychotics, β blockers, codeine and tramadol. Highly polymorphic and not inducible.
- CYP2C9: warfarin (S-enantiomer), phenytoin, many NSAIDs.
- CYP2C19: clopidogrel activation, PPIs, some antidepressants.
- CYP1A2: theophylline, clozapine; induced by smoking.

**Phase II (conjugation)**
- UGTs (glucuronidation): morphine, acetaminophen, bilirubin. UGT1A1 variants matter for irinotecan.
- SULTs (sulfation), NAT2 (acetylation: isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide), GSTs (glutathione), TPMT (thiopurines), COMT (catechols).

**Induction vs inhibition.** Inducers raise enzyme expression through nuclear receptors (PXR, CAR, AhR). The effect builds over days to weeks and fades just as slowly. Examples: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort. Inhibition is usually immediate and competitive (ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir), or time-dependent and irreversible, in which case it persists until new enzyme is made.

**Pharmacogenetics.** Phenotypes range from poor to ultrarapid metabolizers. NAT2 slow acetylators get isoniazid neuropathy and drug-induced lupus more often.

**Development.** Neonates have immature UGT activity; chloramphenicol accumulation causes "gray baby syndrome."

**Enterohepatic recycling.** Glucuronides excreted in bile can be cleaved by gut bacteria, releasing the parent drug for reabsorption and prolonging its action.
levels.phd:
**CYP catalysis.** The P450 cycle binds substrate, reduces the heme iron, binds O2 and adds a second electron (from NADPH–P450 reductase or cytochrome b5), then forms the highly reactive iron(IV)-oxo porphyrin radical cation (**Compound I**). Hydrogen abstraction and "oxygen rebound" yield hydroxylation. The broad, flexible active site of CYP3A4 accommodates large and multiple substrates simultaneously, producing **atypical (non-Michaelis–Menten) kinetics** such as homotropic cooperativity and heteroactivation, which complicate in vitro to in vivo extrapolation.

**Mechanism-based inactivation.** Some substrates are converted into reactive intermediates that destroy the enzyme: covalent heme or apoprotein adducts, or metabolite–intermediate complexes (the nitroso intermediates of macrolides that coordinate the heme). Inhibition then depends on time and persists until new enzyme is synthesized, governed by the enzyme's turnover half-life (roughly a day or more for hepatic CYP3A4, and different for the intestinal pool). Clarithromycin, erythromycin, diltiazem, mibefradil and grapefruit furanocoumarins act this way, which is why their interactions outlast plasma exposure.

**Nuclear receptor induction.** PXR has a large, promiscuous ligand-binding pocket that senses diverse xenobiotics (rifampin, hyperforin from St John's wort) and induces CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C, UGTs and P-gp together. This coordinated induction is why rifampin interactions are so broad. Constitutive androstane receptor (CAR) is activated indirectly by phenobarbital through dephosphorylation. AhR responds to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (smoke, charred food) and induces CYP1A2.

**Bioactivation and toxicity.** Reactive metabolites (quinone imines, epoxides, acyl glucuronides) can covalently modify proteins, causing direct injury or creating neoantigens for immune-mediated idiosyncratic reactions. Medicinal chemists screen for "structural alerts" and glutathione trapping. Total daily body burden matters: idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity is rare for drugs given at low daily amounts, a pattern observed across many drug classes.

**Extrahepatic and microbial metabolism.** Gut bacteria reduce, deconjugate and even directly inactivate drugs (digoxin reduction by Eggerthella lenta; β-glucuronidase-driven irinotecan toxicity), adding a further source of variability.
levels.expert:
**Interactions you must recognize**
- **Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors** (clarithromycin, azole antifungals, ritonavir and cobicistat) can cause dangerous toxicity with simvastatin (rhabdomyolysis), certain calcium channel blockers (hypotension), tacrolimus and cyclosporine (nephrotoxicity), and midazolam (prolonged sedation).
- **Strong inducers** (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) cause treatment failure: hormonal contraceptives, direct oral anticoagulants, many antiretrovirals, tacrolimus. After stopping an inducer, the effect fades over one to two weeks, so levels of co-medications can rise toxically if their doses were increased.
- **Antiepileptics in neurosurgery**: the enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs reduce levels of dexamethasone and many chemotherapy agents used for brain tumors. That is part of why levetiracetam, which has little CYP involvement, is so widely used in neuro-oncology. Valproate inhibits glucuronidation and raises lamotrigine levels, increasing the risk of serious rash.

**Prodrug pitfalls.** CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers can make dangerous amounts of morphine from codeine; deaths in children after tonsillectomy led to codeine contraindications in young patients. CYP2C19 poor metabolizers activate clopidogrel poorly, and some centers genotype patients or choose ticagrelor or prasugrel after stenting. This matters for neurointerventional stents and flow diverters.

**Liver disease.** Cirrhosis reduces phase I oxidation more than glucuronidation, so drugs cleared mainly by glucuronidation (lorazepam, oxazepam) are often chosen over midazolam or diazepam. Reduced first pass in cirrhosis or portosystemic shunting raises oral bioavailability of high-extraction drugs. Coagulation and albumin values are better guides to synthetic function than transaminases.

**Acetaminophen** is a daily tool on surgical wards. Fasting, chronic alcohol use and malnutrition deplete glutathione and lower the margin for toxicity. N-acetylcysteine is most effective when given early, ideally within about eight hours of an acute ingestion.

The attending's habit: for every new drug added, ask whether it is an inducer, an inhibitor or a narrow-therapeutic-index substrate.

keyPoints: Metabolism converts lipophilic drugs into polar, excretable products, mainly in the liver
Phase I: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis (CYP450); Phase II: conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, glutathione, methylation)
CYP3A4 metabolizes the largest share of drugs; CYP2D6 is highly polymorphic
Inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) act over days; inhibitors (azoles, clarithromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit) act quickly
Prodrugs: codeine → morphine (CYP2D6), clopidogrel → active metabolite (CYP2C19)
Acetaminophen overdose → NAPQI; antidote N-acetylcysteine

lessons.title: Elimination and Clearance

levels.kid:
After a medicine has done its job, your body needs to get rid of it. This is called **elimination**.

Your kidneys are like a coffee filter. Blood goes through them, and they filter out leftover medicine into your pee. Some medicine leaves through the liver into your poop instead.

Doctors talk about **clearance**. That means how much blood gets cleaned of medicine every minute, like how fast a pool filter cleans the water. If someone's kidneys are tired or sick, they clean more slowly, so the medicine stays around longer. Then doctors give less of it.
levels.hs:
**Elimination** is the permanent removal of drug from the body, by **metabolism** (changing it) and **excretion** (removing it). The kidneys are the main route of excretion; bile and feces come second. Lungs remove gases such as inhaled anesthetics.

How the kidney handles a drug:
1. **Filtration**: free (unbound) drug is filtered at the glomerulus.
2. **Secretion**: transporters in the tubules actively pump some drugs into the urine (penicillin is a classic example).
3. **Reabsorption**: fat-soluble, uncharged drug can diffuse back into the blood. Changing urine pH can trap drugs in the urine: making urine more alkaline speeds the removal of weak acids such as aspirin (salicylate).

**Clearance (CL)** describes how efficiently the body removes a drug. It is the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time:

CL = rate of elimination ÷ plasma concentration

Total clearance is the sum of renal, hepatic and other clearances.

For most drugs, elimination is **first-order**: a constant **fraction** is removed per unit time, so more drug in the body means more removed. A few drugs saturate their enzymes and switch to **zero-order** elimination: a constant **amount** is removed per unit time no matter how much is there. Phenytoin and high levels of aspirin behave this way, which makes their levels jump unpredictably.

Kidney function is estimated from blood creatinine. When it falls, drugs cleared by the kidneys accumulate unless the dose is reduced.
levels.college:
**Clearance** is the proportionality constant between elimination rate and concentration: rate = CL × C. It is additive across organs: CLtotal = CLrenal + CLhepatic + CLother.

**Organ clearance.** CLorgan = Q × E, where Q is blood flow and E the extraction ratio, (Cin − Cout)/Cin.
- **High-extraction drugs** (E > 0.7: propranolol, lidocaine, morphine, verapamil) are **flow-limited**: their clearance follows hepatic blood flow, and oral bioavailability is low because of first pass.
- **Low-extraction drugs** (E < 0.3: warfarin, phenytoin, diazepam, theophylline) are **capacity-limited**: clearance depends on fu × intrinsic clearance, so enzyme induction or inhibition and protein binding changes matter, while blood flow matters little.

**Renal clearance** = filtration + secretion − reabsorption.
- Filtration clearance = fu × GFR.
- If CLrenal > fu × GFR, net secretion occurs (OAT transporters for anions such as penicillin and methotrexate; OCT2 and MATE for cations such as metformin). Probenecid inhibits OAT and raises penicillin levels.
- If CLrenal < fu × GFR, net reabsorption occurs. Urinary alkalinization (bicarbonate) ion-traps weak acids such as salicylate and phenobarbital; acidification would favor weak bases but is not used clinically.

**Estimating kidney function.** Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance and eGFR equations (CKD-EPI) both rely on steady-state creatinine; they are unreliable when creatinine is changing (acute kidney injury) or muscle mass is unusual.

**Kinetic order.** First-order: rate ∝ concentration; constant fraction per time; constant half-life. Zero-order (saturable, Michaelis–Menten): rate = Vmax × C / (Km + C). When C >> Km, the rate approaches Vmax, a constant amount per time; small dose increases cause disproportionate rises in concentration. Classic examples: phenytoin and high-concentration salicylate.

**Other routes**: biliary excretion (large, polar, often conjugated molecules) with possible enterohepatic recycling; pulmonary excretion of volatile anesthetics; minor routes such as breast milk and sweat.
levels.phd:
**The well-stirred model** links organ clearance to physiology: CLH = QH × fu × CLint / (QH + fu × CLint). When fu × CLint >> QH, CLH approaches QH (flow-limited). When fu × CLint << QH, CLH ≈ fu × CLint (capacity-limited). This single equation predicts which perturbations matter. For a high-extraction drug, induction barely changes IV clearance, but it changes oral exposure, because oral AUC = F × dose / CL, which simplifies to dose / (fu × CLint) regardless of extraction. In other words, **oral exposure always reflects intrinsic clearance**, while IV exposure reflects it only for low-extraction drugs. Alternative models (parallel-tube, dispersion) differ quantitatively for high-extraction drugs, but the qualitative lessons hold.

**Transporter-mediated clearance** adds another layer. In the extended clearance concept, hepatic clearance depends on sinusoidal uptake (OATP1B1/1B3), passive diffusion, metabolism, biliary efflux (MRP2, BCRP, BSEP) and basolateral efflux. When uptake is rate-limiting, OATP inhibition (cyclosporine, rifampin given acutely) raises plasma levels of statins even without CYP involvement. SLCO1B1 polymorphisms (such as c.521T>C) increase simvastatin acid exposure and myopathy risk.

**Renal secretion** can clear even highly protein-bound drugs efficiently, because transporters strip drug from albumin as the unbound fraction is removed. Drug–drug interactions at OCT2/MATE (trimethoprim, cimetidine, dolutegravir) also block creatinine secretion, raising serum creatinine without changing true GFR. This is a classic interpretive trap.

**Nonlinear elimination.** For Michaelis–Menten drugs, the apparent half-life increases with concentration, time to steady state lengthens as the dosing rate approaches Vmax, and at rates above Vmax no steady state exists. Target-mediated drug disposition, common with monoclonal antibodies, produces faster clearance at low concentrations, where binding to the target is a significant sink, and slower clearance once the target is saturated.

**Augmented renal clearance** (above-normal creatinine clearance in young, critically ill patients after trauma, TBI or SAH) is underrecognized and leads to subtherapeutic exposure of renally cleared antibiotics and antiseizure drugs.
levels.expert:
**Renal dosing is daily practice.** Renally cleared drugs that commonly need adjustment include many antibiotics (aminoglycosides, vancomycin, many β-lactams), levetiracetam, gabapentin and pregabalin, enoxaparin, direct oral anticoagulants (especially dabigatran), lithium, metformin and digoxin. Accumulation of renally cleared metabolites causes trouble too: morphine-6-glucuronide (sedation and respiratory depression in renal failure), the meperidine metabolite normeperidine (seizures) and gabapentinoids (confusion, myoclonus). In kidney failure, opioids with fewer active renal metabolites are usually preferred.

**Don't trust a changing creatinine.** In acute kidney injury, serum creatinine lags the true GFR, so estimates overestimate function as kidneys fail and underestimate it during recovery. Use clinical judgment, urine output and drug levels where available.

**Neurocritical patients often clear drugs faster than expected.** Young patients with TBI or subarachnoid hemorrhage commonly have augmented renal clearance, especially with hyperdynamic circulation and fluid loading. Standard regimens of levetiracetam, vancomycin or β-lactams can then produce low levels, a risk for breakthrough seizures or treatment failure. Measured urine creatinine clearance and therapeutic drug monitoring help.

**Dialysis.** Whether a drug is removed by hemodialysis depends on its size, protein binding and Vd. Small, poorly protein-bound drugs with small Vd (lithium, salicylate, toxic alcohols, metformin, valproate when levels are very high) are dialyzable, which is why dialysis is an antidote for some poisonings. Drugs with very large Vd (digoxin, tricyclics, amiodarone) are not meaningfully removed.

**Zero-order traps.** Phenytoin's saturable metabolism means a small increase in the dosing rate can push a patient from therapeutic to toxic levels (nystagmus, ataxia, confusion). Increase cautiously and recheck levels, which take longer than usual to settle.

**Creatinine pitfalls.** Trimethoprim and some other drugs block creatinine secretion, raising serum creatinine without true kidney injury.

keyPoints: Elimination = metabolism + excretion; kidney is the main excretory organ
Renal handling = glomerular filtration (free drug) + tubular secretion − reabsorption
Clearance = elimination rate / plasma concentration; total CL = sum of organ clearances
Organ CL = blood flow × extraction ratio; high-extraction drugs are flow-limited
First-order: constant fraction per time; zero-order: constant amount per time (phenytoin, high-level salicylate)
Urinary alkalinization traps weak acids (salicylate, phenobarbital)

test.q: Clearance is best defined as:
choices: The time for concentration to fall by half
The amount of drug removed per day
The volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time
test.explain: CL = elimination rate / concentration, expressed as volume per time.

test.q: Which form of a drug is filtered at the glomerulus?
test.explain: Albumin is too large to be filtered, so only unbound drug is filtered.

test.q: In first-order elimination:
choices: A constant amount is removed per unit time
A constant fraction is removed per unit time
test.explain: First-order elimination removes a constant fraction, so half-life is constant.

test.q: Which drug classically shows zero-order (saturable) elimination at therapeutic levels?
test.explain: Phenytoin's metabolism saturates within the therapeutic range.

test.q: Alkalinizing the urine with sodium bicarbonate speeds elimination of:
test.explain: In alkaline urine, weak acids are ionized, trapped and excreted.

test.q: Probenecid raises penicillin levels by:
choices: Inducing CYP3A4, which converts penicillin into a longer-acting form
Inhibiting renal tubular secretion via organic anion transporters
Increasing penicillin absorption by slowing transit through the gut
Displacing penicillin from albumin so more free drug circulates
test.explain: Probenecid blocks OAT-mediated secretion of penicillin.

test.q: Organ clearance equals blood flow multiplied by the ___ ratio.
test.explain: CLorgan = Q × E.

test.q: Total body clearance is the ___ of the clearances of each eliminating organ.
test.explain: Clearances are additive: CLtotal = CLrenal + CLhepatic + CLother.

test.q: A high-extraction drug such as lidocaine has hepatic clearance that mainly depends on:
test.explain: High-extraction drugs are flow-limited: CL approaches hepatic blood flow.

test.q: Which lab value is most commonly used to estimate kidney function for drug dosing?
test.explain: Creatinine-based equations (Cockcroft–Gault, CKD-EPI) estimate creatinine clearance or GFR.

test.q: Name the renal process in which transporters actively pump drug into the tubular fluid. (one word)
test.explain: Tubular secretion via OATs and OCTs adds to filtration.

test.q: In zero-order elimination, a constant ___ of drug is removed per unit time: amount or fraction?
test.explain: Zero-order = constant amount; first-order = constant fraction.

kidTest.q: Getting rid of medicine is called:
kidTest.explain: Elimination removes drug from the body.

kidTest.q: Your kidneys are like a:
kidTest.explain: Kidneys filter blood and put leftover medicine into urine.

kidTest.q: If kidneys are tired or sick, medicine stays around:
kidTest.explain: Slower cleaning means the drug lasts longer.

kidTest.q: Some medicine leaves the body through the liver into:
kidTest.explain: Biliary excretion ends up in feces.

kidTest.q: Medicine filtered by the kidneys leaves the body in ___. (one word)
kidTest.explain: The kidneys excrete drugs into urine.

advancedTest.q: A young patient with subarachnoid hemorrhage has breakthrough seizures on a standard levetiracetam regimen with normal creatinine. A likely pharmacokinetic reason is:
advancedTest.explain: Hyperdynamic, young neurocritical patients often clear renally eliminated drugs faster than normal.

advancedTest.q: Trimethoprim raises serum creatinine without lowering true GFR because it:
choices: Increases muscle breakdown, which releases creatinine
Blocks glomerular filtration of creatinine molecules

IV clearance rather than oral exposure
advancedTest.explain: IV CL ≈ hepatic blood flow, but oral AUC = dose / (fu × CLint) and falls with induction.

advancedTest.explain: Digoxin's very large Vd and tissue binding mean little is in the plasma for dialysis to remove.

lessons.title: Half-Life, Steady State and Loading Doses

levels.kid:
**Half-life** is how long it takes for half of a medicine to leave your body. Imagine a big cookie. Every hour, you eat half of what's left. Soon there's just a tiny crumb.

If you take medicine again and again, it builds up until the amount coming in equals the amount going out. That's called **steady state**, like a bathtub with the tap on and the drain open, where the water stays at the same level.

It takes about four or five half-lives to get there. If doctors need the medicine to work right away, they can give a bigger first dose to fill the tub fast.
levels.hs:
The **half-life (t½)** is the time it takes for the plasma concentration of a drug to fall by half. For first-order drugs, it stays the same no matter the starting level. After one half-life 50% remains, after two 25%, after three 12.5%, and after **four to five half-lives** almost all of the drug (about 94–97%) is gone.

**Steady state.** When a drug is given repeatedly or as a continuous infusion, it accumulates until the rate going in equals the rate going out. That balance is steady state. Two big rules:
- **Time to reach steady state depends only on half-life**: about four to five half-lives, whatever the dose.
- **The level at steady state depends on the dosing rate and clearance**: double the dosing rate and the steady-state level doubles (for first-order drugs).

So a drug with a long half-life, like amiodarone (weeks), would take a very long time to reach its target level.

**Loading dose.** To get to the target level quickly, a larger first dose can be given to "fill up" the volume of distribution at once. After that, smaller **maintenance doses** replace what is eliminated. The loading amount depends on the **volume of distribution**, and the maintenance amount depends on **clearance**.

Half-life also guides how often a drug is given and how long its effects last after stopping it, which matters when planning surgery or switching medicines.
levels.college:
**Half-life is a derived parameter.** For first-order, one-compartment kinetics:

t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL   (0.693 = ln 2)

and the elimination rate constant k = CL / Vd = 0.693 / t½. Half-life therefore rises if Vd increases (more drug hidden in tissue) or clearance falls (kidney or liver failure). Two drugs can share a half-life but differ completely in clearance.

**Accumulation and steady state.** With a constant infusion, the concentration rises as C(t) = Css × (1 − e^(−kt)): 50% of Css after one half-life, about 75% after two, about 87.5% after three, and about 94% after four.

Steady-state concentration: Css = dosing rate × F / CL. For intermittent dosing, the average Css = F × dose / (CL × τ), where τ is the dosing interval. Peak–trough fluctuation depends on τ relative to t½. The accumulation factor is 1 / (1 − e^(−kτ)).

**Loading dose** = Ctarget × Vd / F. It is set by Vd, so it is generally not reduced in renal failure (Vd is usually unchanged), whereas the maintenance dosing rate (CL × Ctarget / F) is reduced when clearance falls.

**Elimination after stopping.** Washout also takes about four to five half-lives, which guides switching between interacting drugs and timing before surgery.

**Multicompartment drugs.** After an IV bolus, concentration falls fast at first (distribution, α phase) and then more slowly (elimination, β phase). The **terminal half-life** may overstate how quickly the effect wears off for drugs whose effect tracks the central compartment, or understate the accumulation of drugs with deep tissue stores.

**Context-sensitive half-time** is the time for plasma concentration to fall by 50% after stopping an infusion of a given duration. It grows with infusion length for drugs such as fentanyl (which saturates peripheral tissues) but stays short for remifentanil (rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases).
levels.phd:
**The half-life is a hybrid of two independent physiological variables.** Clearance reflects the capacity of eliminating organs; Vd reflects partitioning between plasma and tissues. Changes in half-life are therefore ambiguous unless you know which variable moved. Aging, for instance, raises the half-life of diazepam mostly by increasing its Vd (more adipose tissue), with relatively little change in clearance, so its steady-state concentration for a given dosing rate barely changes. Only the time to get there, and to wash out, lengthens. By contrast, renal impairment raises the half-life of gentamicin through falling clearance, which raises Css unless the dosing rate is cut.

**Effective half-life.** For multicompartment drugs, the terminal half-life may represent a small fraction of the AUC. The effective (or accumulation) half-life, derived from the observed accumulation ratio at steady state, often predicts both the time to steady state and peak–trough behavior better. Drugs like amiodarone have terminal half-lives of weeks to months because of deep tissue stores, but much of their clinical exposure behaves according to shorter phases, and loading strategies are designed around those.

**Hysteresis.** Effect often lags plasma concentration because drug must reach a biophase (the effect site). Effect-compartment models introduce ke0, the first-order rate constant for equilibration between plasma and effect site. The **time to peak effect** after a bolus (fast for propofol and remifentanil, slower for morphine because of poor BBB permeability) determines how quickly re-dosing can be judged. Proteresis and indirect response models (drug affecting the synthesis or loss of a mediator, as with warfarin and clotting factors) add further dissociation between concentration and effect. Warfarin's effect follows the half-lives of clotting factors, with factor VII falling first and factor II last, rather than the drug's own half-life.

**Nonlinear kinetics** break all of these rules. For Michaelis–Menten drugs, half-life increases with concentration, and the time to reach steady state grows as dosing approaches Vmax. The "four to five half-lives" rule becomes misleading, which is why phenytoin levels can keep drifting for weeks after a change.
levels.expert:
**Loading doses save lives when time matters.** In status epilepticus, a loading dose of fosphenytoin, levetiracetam or valproate is given to reach effective concentrations within minutes, because waiting several half-lives for accumulation is unacceptable. The same logic applies to amiodarone in arrhythmias, digoxin when rapid rate control is needed, and vancomycin in serious infections. In renal failure, give a normal loading dose (set by Vd) and then reduce or space maintenance doses (set by clearance).

**Timing drug levels.** Therapeutic drug monitoring is meaningful at steady state, roughly four to five half-lives after a start or change, unless a loading dose was given. Trough levels are drawn just before the next dose. Drawing a level too early, or during the distribution phase (digoxin within about six hours of a dose), produces misleading results. For vancomycin, many centers now target the AUC rather than the trough, estimated with Bayesian software.

**Washout before procedures.** Stopping an anticoagulant before neurosurgery depends on its half-life and on the patient's renal function. Dabigatran, which is mostly renally cleared, needs a longer hold when kidney function is reduced. Long half-life drugs and irreversible inhibitors, whose effect outlasts the drug, require their own plans.

**Context-sensitive half-time in the neuro-ICU.** After days of a fentanyl or midazolam infusion, sedation can persist long after stopping, confounding brain death evaluation or neurologic examination. Propofol and dexmedetomidine wear off more predictably, and remifentanil offset stays short regardless of duration. Before a formal brain death evaluation, enough time must pass for sedatives to clear, sometimes several half-lives adjusted for organ dysfunction and hypothermia, or drug levels must be checked.

**Steady-state reasoning for interactions.** After starting an inhibitor, a substrate's level climbs over four to five of its new, longer half-lives. That is why toxicity can appear days later rather than immediately. Monitor through the whole climb, not just the first day.

keyPoints: Half-life (t½) = 0.693 × Vd / CL; it is a derived parameter
About 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state, and 4–5 to wash out
Time to steady state depends only on t½; the steady-state level depends on dosing rate and clearance
Loading dose = target concentration × Vd / F (set by Vd)
Maintenance dosing rate = CL × target concentration / F (set by clearance)
Context-sensitive half-time grows with infusion duration for drugs like fentanyl

test.q: Approximately how many half-lives does it take to reach steady state with repeated dosing?
test.explain: After 4–5 half-lives, concentration is about 94–97% of steady state.

test.q: The half-life of a first-order drug equals:
test.explain: t½ = ln 2 × Vd / CL, so it rises with larger Vd or lower clearance.

test.q: Doubling the dosing rate of a first-order drug will:
choices: Double the steady-state concentration without changing time to steady state
Double the half-life and double the time it takes to reach steady state
Have no effect on concentration because clearance rises in proportion
Halve the time to steady state while keeping the same plateau level
test.explain: Css is proportional to dosing rate; time to steady state depends only on half-life.

test.q: A loading dose is determined mainly by:
test.explain: Loading dose = target concentration × Vd / F.

test.q: A patient develops kidney failure. For a renally cleared drug, what usually changes?
choices: The drug's volume of distribution shrinks markedly as renal function worsens
The maintenance dosing rate should be reduced because clearance falls
The loading dose should fall sharply because the drug distributes poorly
Clearance stays stable, since the liver takes over clearing the drug
test.explain: Clearance falls, so maintenance dosing is reduced; the loading dose (set by Vd) is usually unchanged.

test.q: After three half-lives, what percentage of the original drug remains (first-order)?
Half-life equals 0.693 times Vd divided by ___.
test.explain: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL.

test.q: The time to reach steady state depends only on the drug's ___.
test.explain: Dose size changes the steady-state level, not the time to reach it.

test.q: Steady state is reached when:
choices: Plasma concentration first falls below the effective level
The rate of drug input equals the rate of elimination
The whole dose has been fully absorbed from the gut
Peak plasma concentration is at its highest possible level
test.explain: At steady state, input and elimination rates are balanced.

test.q: Why does sedation persist after a long fentanyl infusion but not after a long remifentanil infusion?
choices: Remifentanil is excreted unchanged by the kidneys within minutes, while fentanyl needs conversion by CYP2D6 in the liver
Fentanyl is poorly lipophilic, so it is trapped in plasma for hours, whereas remifentanil quickly crosses into fat and muscle
Remifentanil has a much larger Vd than fentanyl, which dilutes it so far below the effective level that patients wake quickly
Fentanyl saturates peripheral tissues, giving a long context-sensitive half-time; remifentanil is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases
test.explain: Context-sensitive half-time rises with infusion length for fentanyl but stays short for remifentanil.

test.q: What is the name for a larger initial dose given to reach the target concentration quickly? (two words)
test.explain: A loading dose fills the volume of distribution at once.

test.q: The maintenance dosing rate is set mainly by which PK parameter? (one word)
test.explain: Maintenance rate = CL × target concentration / F.

kidTest.q: Half-life is how long it takes for ___ of the medicine to leave.
kidTest.explain: Half-life = time for half of the drug to go.

kidTest.q: Steady state is like a bathtub where the water:
kidTest.explain: Input equals output, so the level stays steady.

kidTest.q: A bigger first dose to fill the tub fast is called a:
kidTest.explain: A loading dose reaches the target level quickly.

kidTest.q: About how many half-lives does it take to fill the tub?
kidTest.explain: About 4–5 half-lives to steady state.

kidTest.q: If you eat half the cookie each hour, after two hours you have one ___ left.
kidTest.explain: Half of a half is a quarter.

advancedTest.q: In an elderly patient, diazepam's half-life is prolonged mostly because Vd increases. What happens to its steady-state concentration at the same dosing rate?
choices: It halves, because the drug is spread through a larger volume of tissue
It doubles because longer half-life directly implies greater steady-state exposure
Little change, because Css depends on clearance; only the time to steady state lengthens
It becomes unpredictable, as elderly patients switch to zero-order kinetics
advancedTest.explain: Css = dosing rate / CL. A larger Vd lengthens t½ (time to steady state and washout) without changing Css if clearance is unchanged.

advancedTest.q: Warfarin's anticoagulant effect lags its plasma concentration mainly because:
choices: It needs activation by CYP2D6 into an active metabolite before it works
It has a terminal half-life of several months, so levels rise very slowly
Its effect depends on the decay of existing clotting factors, an indirect response
It is poorly absorbed, so effective plasma levels take days to build up
advancedTest.explain: Warfarin blocks synthesis of new factors; the effect follows the clearance of existing factors (VII first, II last).

advancedTest.q: Why might a digoxin level drawn two hours after a dose be misleading?
choices: Digoxin concentration is too low to measure accurately within hours
It reflects the distribution phase, before plasma and tissue equilibrate
Digoxin needs conversion to an active metabolite before levels matter
It follows zero-order kinetics, so early levels underestimate exposure
advancedTest.explain: Digoxin distributes slowly into tissue; levels should be drawn after distribution is complete.

advancedTest.q: After a CYP inhibitor is added, a substrate with a newly prolonged half-life reaches its new steady state:
choices: After 4–5 of its new, longer half-lives, so toxicity may appear days later
Immediately, because inhibition raises concentrations within the first hour
A plateau is delayed indefinitely because the inhibited drug keeps accumulating
After one half-life of the original drug, regardless of the new half-life
advancedTest.explain: Time to steady state follows the new t½, so concentrations climb over days.
